name: The Seurasaari Anthill Pine

location.address: Seurasaari Open-Air Museum, in the yard behind the Yusupoff stable (Jusupoffin talli)

access: Seurasaari island is free to walk year-round, but this pine stands in the yard of the Yusupoff stable inside the Seurasaari Open-Air Museum's fenced grounds, which charge admission (adult ~14 EUR) when the museum is open, 15 May to 15 September. Outside the season the fenced yards are not staffed; treat as paid entry in season.
transport: Bus 24 to the Seurasaari terminus, then a 5-10 minute walk across the footbridge to the museum area
verify_notes: Register entry (finland-helsinki-luonnonmuistomerkit.json, register_id 24, huom: protected by city board decision, not under the Nature Conservation Act). City of Helsinki natural-monuments page and its 2006 street & park department Seurasaari report (hel.fi/static/hkr/julkaisut/seurasaari/seurasaari_raportti.pdf) both describe the same tree in detail: protected by Helsinki City Board decision 16 Feb 1956 (section 498); base circumference was 280 cm at protection in 1956, grown to 307 cm by a 2003 measurement (girth_cm recorded is the 2003 base-circumference figure, NOT a standard breast-height girth, so do not treat it as directly comparable to DBH-based girths elsewhere in the database); approx. 20 m tall (2003). Registered as "the second thickest unbranched pine tree in Greater Helsinki" per the city’s own register data (a superlative from the source, repeated as such, per hard rule 8). Notable feature: an anthill has spread from the tree’s roots into cracks in the trunk, and a birch seedling has rooted in a hole in the trunk about 5 m up. FLAGGED because both sources trace to the City of Helsinki’s own records (the municipal register and the city’s own published report/webpage); an independent (non-city) corroborating source was searched for (Finnish Wikipedia's Seurasaari article, nature blogs, Theseus thesis on the Yusupoff stable) and not found within the time budget. No age given by either source; base-girth measurement is not a reliable basis for a standard growth-rate age estimate, so age_estimate is left empty rather than guessed. Alive: no post-2003 confirmation found; the tree is not confirmed alive in the last few years, which is the other reason for flagging alongside the single-institution sourcing. why_go: an unusually thick, city-recognised pine growing an anthill straight out of its own bark, tucked in the yard of a 1842 stable moved to the island in 1916; a small, specific find inside a well-known museum rather than a generic old pine.

name: The Tullisaari Burl Pine

location.address: Eastern end of Kumianpää, a path branching east off Henrik Borgströmintie, Laajasalo

access: Free. Stands beside a public recreational path (the eastern end of Kumianpää, off Henrik Borgströmintie); no ticket or gate.
transport: Bus from central Helsinki to Laajasalo (roughly 20 minutes), then a short walk to Kumianpää
verify_notes: Two sources: (1) City of Helsinki natural-monuments register/page (register_id from finland-helsinki-luonnonmuistomerkit.json, nimi "Mukuramänty, Tullisaari"): protected by the Provincial Government of Uusimaa, 20 September 1956 (decision No 8805); 2003 measurement 19 m tall, 175 cm circumference (225 cm including the burl growth). (2) Laajasalo-Degero Seura ry (independent local residents' association, not a city source), whose own nature page names "mukuramänty Kumianpään itäpäässä" as one of Laajasalo's 7 protected natural monuments (of Helsinki's 33 total), independently confirming the tree's existence and exact location. Species: Pinus sylvestris f. gibberosa, a rare naturally occurring burl/gnarl growth-form of Scots pine found in southern and central Finland (cross-checked against a 2014 Yle news piece on a comparable specimen in Hausjarvi, which describes the form and notes such trees are usually under 10 m tall, making this 19 m specimen unusually large for the type). No age recorded by either source and the unusual growth form makes standard girth-based age estimation unreliable, so age_estimate is left empty. FLAGGED because no recent (post-2003) dated confirmation of the tree still standing was found within the time budget; the location itself (public path, residents' association actively naming it) is solid, but "alive now" rests on a 2003 measurement plus a undated modern reference from the local association's page. why_go: not just an old pine but a genetically rare form, its whole trunk, branches and roots gnarled with burls, growing twice the height these trees normally reach; a five-minute detour off a public path in the Tullisaari/Laajasalo cluster where the willow, lime and oak already published sit within the same walk.
